title: Renner v. Kehl
lead: Buyers and sellers mistakenly believed desert leaseholds had enough groundwater for commercial jojoba, allowing rescission but requiring restitution of benefits rather than reimbursement of every development expense.

actors.name: Roy Renner, Lawrence Colton, and Kofa Farms
Vice Chief Justice Gordon
actors.role: Author of the unanimous Arizona Supreme Court opinion

proceedings: Bench trial granted rescission and $309,849.84 plus costs and fees; Court of Appeals affirmed; Supreme Court upheld rescission, reversed the expenditure-based recovery in part, and remanded for restitution accounting.
limits: Sellers supplied no trial record on their evidentiary challenge, requiring a presumption supporting the findings. The report has inconsistent fractional development figures; the aggregate award is reported as $309,849.84. No fraud or misrepresentation was found.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Both sides assumed the desert tract could support the planned crop
sections.cue: Start with the lease sale and the material assumption.
paragraphs: The Kehls and Moyles held state agricultural-development leases on 2,262 acres of unimproved desert near Yuma. Instead of developing the land, they offered their interests for sale. Roy Renner, Lawrence Colton, and Kofa Farms wanted property for large-scale commercial jojoba cultivation. Their agent knew that business, and adequate water was a condition of the buyers’ interest.

Both sides believed the tract had suitable soil and climate and enough accessible groundwater for the venture. On June 5, 1981, the buyers agreed to pay $222,200, paid $80,200 down, and promised annual installments for the balance. Beginning that November, they developed the tract and drilled five test wells. None supplied water of sufficient quality or quantity for commercial jojoba. After spending roughly $229,000, the buyers concluded the aquifer was inadequate, abandoned the project, and sued to rescind. The sellers counterclaimed for the unpaid balance.

sections.title: The trial court unwound the bargain and reimbursed development spending
sections.cue: Separate the right to rescind from the amount recoverable.
paragraphs: Following an October 1983 bench trial, the trial court entered findings and an order in January 1984 allowing rescission for mutual mistake and failure of consideration. It required reassignment of the leases and awarded the buyers $309,849.84, consisting of the down payment and development expenditures, plus costs and attorney’s fees. The Court of Appeals affirmed by memorandum decision on December 17, 1985.

The sellers challenged both rescission and consequential damages in the Arizona Supreme Court. They also disputed the evidentiary support for the findings, but supplied no trial record. Because appellants had responsibility for an adequate record, the reviewing court presumed substantial support for the findings and a proper exercise of discretion.

sections.title: The groundwater mistake went to the basis of the transaction
sections.cue: Explain why unsuccessful investigation did not itself allocate the risk.
paragraphs: Vice Chief Justice Gordon’s opinion upheld rescission under Arizona mutual-mistake doctrine and Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 152. The trial court found that the transaction would not have occurred unless both sides believed jojoba could be grown economically. Adequate water was therefore a material basic assumption, not an incidental preference. The error concerned an existing underground supply, rather than later market changes or disappointing profits.

The court did not treat the buyers’ unsuccessful drilling as proof that they consciously assumed all groundwater risk. Its second footnote emphasized that failure to investigate thoroughly did not itself defeat rescission when the risk had not been allocated and the shared mistake concerned a material basic assumption. The sellers’ missing record also constrained their attempt to overturn the factual premise.

sections.title: An innocent seller did not have to absorb every reliance expense
sections.cue: Distinguish the precedents involving wrongdoing from this mistake.
paragraphs: The Court of Appeals had relied on Fousel, a rescission case allowing incidental or consequential damages, on the theory that rescission plus expenses did not duplicate recovery. Gordon distinguished it because Fousel involved fraud and breach; the associated Jennings authority likewise concerned restoration for a defrauded party. Here the trial court expressly found no fraud or misrepresentation by the sellers or their agents.

Reimbursing all development losses in this fault-free mutual-mistake setting would shift the entire risk to the sellers. The opinion used “consequential” or “incidental” damages to describe these reliance expenses. That label did not change the distinction between compensating everything the buyers spent and returning benefits the sellers received. The court rejected the former measure here, while preserving restitution under § 376 to prevent unjust enrichment.

sections.title: The remand required a benefit-based accounting
sections.cue: End with the formula and the partial disposition.
paragraphs: The buyers had to return the leasehold interests, with that return properly conditioned on restitution. They were entitled to their down payment and any enhancement in the returned property’s value attributable to their work, less the fair rental value of their occupancy. Conversely, the sellers could not retain improvements’ value without accounting for that benefit.

Under § 371(b), the measure was the increase in the recipient’s property or interests, not the developer’s expenditures. Costly or unsuccessful development therefore did not necessarily produce an equivalent restitution award. The trial court needed to determine enhancement and rental value on remand.

On June 25, 1986, Gordon, Holohan, Hays, Cameron, and Feldman unanimously affirmed the trial court in part and reversed in part, approved the appellate decision in part and vacated it in part, and remanded under that formula. Rescission survived; the complete $309,849.84 award did not.
